source.title: Adapter Merging with Centroid Prototype Mapping for Scalable Class-Incremental Learning
source.authors: Takuma Fukuda; Hiroshi Kera; Kazuhiko Kawamoto

record.tranche_reason: The study measures whether prototype representations from different task-adapter subspaces can be aligned using a centroid mapping. This bears on representation mapping, but uses a task-specific cosine-similarity analysis rather than the original sources' methods.
record.gate_note: The relevant results are prototype cosine similarities across adapter subspaces, including mapped-versus-unmapped comparisons. Accuracy, inference-time, and adapter-loss-landscape results do not directly measure the claim's representation alignment and are not rows.
record.test_reason: A continual-learning method paper. Its cosine-similarity results compare the authors' own centroid prototype mapping with unmapped prototypes and with SDC. The prototypes come from successive merged-adapter states of one pretrained ViT-B/16, with adapters sharing initial weights. They are not independently trained models, different seeds or different architectures, so no version is tested. Convergent Learning (an original source) is cited only as a reference on aligning models for weight averaging.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly off-focus. The authors' main conclusion is about their method: ACMap, which merges task-specific adapters into one adapter with centroid prototype mapping, matches state-of-the-art exemplar-free class-incremental accuracy at constant inference time (39x faster than EASE at 40 tasks). Centroid mapping is shown to align earlier prototypes better than no mapping or SDC. They note limits on VTAB's heterogeneous tasks and little benefit from adapters on CUB.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a centroid-based prototype shift and cosine similarity between task-adapter subspaces in class-incremental vision learning, rather than the original sources' representation-convergence methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Alignment varies with task proximity: the paper reports poor alignment for task-1 prototypes in later subspaces but high cosine similarity when task-5 prototypes are used; CUB has high similarity even without mapping.

fits_no_version.finding: Prototypes of early classes drift across successive merged-adapter states of one ViT-B/16 (cosine similarity falls toward roughly 0.8 over tasks). A single affine centroid shift largely restores alignment (Figs 4, 6, G, H).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Representation drift within one pretrained model under sequential adapter fine-tuning is approximately a shared translation across classes.

record.problems: The relevant cosine-similarity results are plotted rather than tabulated, with no reported uncertainty for these measurements. The alignment analysis is limited to prototype vectors and task adapters in vision CIL, not general representations across independently trained models.

untested.parts: No scale sweep or comparison of independently trained models.
No comparison across random seeds of independently trained networks.
No mapping between different models' representations; only drift correction within one model's adapter updates.
No comparison of similarity metrics or input choices.
No analysis of the extent or causes of cross-model convergence.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'tests/T2, supports V4' reading overstates the study's relevance. The 'subspaces' are states of a single model being fine-tuned from a shared adapter initialization. Same-model drift correction is not evidence about convergence or interchangeability between independently trained models.

versions.untested_parts: No scale or capability sweep, or comparison of independently trained models with different architectures, objectives, or data.
No paired image-caption or vision-language alignment.
No study of features or shared subspaces across random initialization seeds; task adapters share an initialization.
Tests centroid prototype mapping between task-adapter subspaces in vision CIL, not general linear maps, stitching, relative representations, or unpaired mapping across independently trained models.
No interpretable feature, neuron, SAE-feature, or circuit comparison.
Uses cosine similarity; does not compare similarity metrics, metric settings, or in-distribution versus out-of-distribution inputs as a test of metric dependence.
Does not test whether shared data or objectives explain convergence instead of a common model of reality, nor whether alignment plateaus or remains incomplete in the sense of this version.

rows.subject: ViT-B/16
rows.stage_stated: Task-specific adapters trained for CIL; adapters are merged
rows.operation_detail: Cosine similarity of centroid-mapped first-task prototypes to true first-task prototypes in later merged-adapter subspaces
rows.measure: Cosine similarity between mapped and true prototypes
rows.baseline: Unmapped first-task prototypes, shown as semi-transparent curves
rows.value: figure only; text says mapped prototypes consistently have higher cosine similarity than unmapped prototypes
rows.note: The text says mapping effectively aligns prototypes with the true prototypes. Figure H includes additional experiments; this configuration also appears in Figure 6.
rows.check: Measures the authors' own method (centroid mapping) against unmapped prototypes within one model's sequential adapter states. Not a mapping between different models' representations as V4 names. Figure-only.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Centroid prototype mapping across the tested CIL datasets and task configurations
reader_labels.reason: The authors report that mapped prototypes have higher cosine similarity to true prototypes than unmapped ones across the datasets; see r1-r9.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: CUB B0 Inc10 and unmapped prototypes from tasks closer to the current task
reader_labels.reason: Unmapped prototypes already show high similarity on CUB, and task-5 prototypes retain high similarity in later subspaces; the need and benefit of mapping are therefore not uniform. See r9, r14, r15.
